cards.label: Case Study
cards.title: Testing Decisions
cards.summary: A five-part rule for ordering release testing, a four-line summary for the person who decides to ship, and a measurement that surprised me.
cards.visualAlt: Looping illustration: test time split 60, 30 and 10 percent across critical, medium and low flows, then a four-line release summary.
cards.code: Plan 8 hours: critical 60%, medium 30%, low 10%. Then write the four-line release summary.
cards.oneLiner: 75% fewer live-site test runs on pull requests, and a four-line summary for whoever decides to ship.

testing.chat: Plan 8 hours: critical 60%, medium 30%, low 10%. Then write the four-line summary.
testing.alt: Animated result: eight hours split 4.8 critical, 2.4 medium and 0.8 low, a pull request runs 16 of 65 browser tests, then a four-line summary.

timebar.title: An 8-hour release
timebar.alt: Eight hours split 60, 30 and 10 percent: 4.8 hours for critical flows, 2.4 for medium and 0.8 for low, then a four-line summary for the person deciding to ship.

segments.name: Critical
segments.line: Flows that touch revenue or the core business process. If these break, the release is not shippable.

segments.name: Medium
segments.line: Checked next, only once every critical flow is done.

segments.name: Low
segments.line: Whatever time is left. Some may not be reached, and the summary says so.

summary.title: Then four lines for the person deciding to ship
lines: Critical: done. Medium: done. Low: partly done.
Two low-priority screens, not reached: time ran out.
One medium issue, does not block.
Ship. If the medium issue turns out to affect payments, hold.
summary.note: Example wording, not a real release.

scope.alt: What the test-scope script runs for six cases: smoke tests only for a plain pull request, the full suite for every other case.
scope.asOf: As the script stood on 10 November 2026.

events.text: Push to main, nightly run or manual run

check.text: Changes the tests, how they run, or has the full-regression label?

scenarios.label: A pull request
scenarios.why: A plain pull request runs only the smoke tests, 16 of the 65 browser tests.

scenarios.label: It touches the tests
scenarios.why: A change to the tests, or to how they run, could break the smoke set itself, so everything runs.

scenarios.label: It has the full-regression label
scenarios.why: The label is how I ask for everything on a pull request.

scenarios.label: A push to main
scenarios.why: Pushes to the main branch always run everything.

scenarios.label: The nightly run
scenarios.why: Nightly and manual runs always run everything.

scenarios.label: It cannot tell
scenarios.why: Running too much costs a minute; running too little lets a broken test merge. So when the script cannot tell what changed, it runs everything.

cards.label: Case Study
cards.title: Rejected-Ticket Triage
cards.summary: One question settles whether a rejected ticket needs a better requirement or a fix in the code, and gives each answer an owner.
cards.visualAlt: Looping illustration: a rejected sample ticket is asked whether the acceptance criteria already say it, then goes to the requirement owner as a spec gap or back to the developer as an implementation gap.
cards.code: Quote the criterion the build breaks. If there is none, label it a spec gap and write the missing criterion.
cards.oneLiner: One question tells a missing requirement from a missed fix, so a rejected ticket goes to the right person first.

scope.alt: Six sample rejected tickets: three go back to the developer as implementation gaps and three go to the requirement owner as spec gaps.
scope.asOf: Six made-up tickets for an imaginary report export.

check.text: Do the acceptance criteria already say it?

outcomes.detail: Back to the developer, with the criterion that fails
To the requirement owner, with the missing criterion

scenarios.label: Export button does nothing
scenarios.why: The criteria say the button exports a CSV file. It does not, so the build missed something that was written down.

scenarios.label: Export has no totals row
scenarios.why: The criteria never mention totals. The developer built what was written, so the owner fixes the requirement first.

scenarios.label: Dates show in the wrong format
scenarios.why: The criteria say dates are shown as year-month-day. The build shows something else.

scenarios.label: Customer expected a PDF
scenarios.why: The criteria say CSV. The wish is new, so the owner adds it to the criteria or logs a new request.

scenarios.label: A large file freezes the export
scenarios.why: Nothing says how many rows it must handle. Ask the owner for a number, then test against it.

scenarios.label: Columns are in the wrong order
scenarios.why: The criteria list the column order. The build does not follow it.

cards.label: Case Study
cards.title: Release Notes to a Change Brief
cards.imageAlt: Title card: Release Notes to a Change Brief
cards.summary: One question decides which changes in a release a customer hears about, and how: an action box, one line, or the release notes only.
cards.visualAlt: Looping illustration of a pull request: a reviewer asks of every line of a change brief whether the customer has to do something, so each visible change is marked as an action box or one plain line, while a change nobody can see skips the question and stays in the release notes.
cards.code: Put every change that needs the customer to act in a box at the top, with what to do and by when. Give each other visible change one plain line. Leave out changes a customer cannot see, and list what you left out.
cards.oneLiner: One question turns a long list of release notes into a one-page brief that puts what the customer must do first.

scope.alt: Six sample changes in an imaginary release: two need the customer to act and go in an action box, three get one line, and one stays in the release notes.
scope.asOf: Six made-up changes for an imaginary booking app.

check.text: Does the customer have to do something?
check.skipped: Not asked: nobody outside can see it

outcomes.detail: At the top, with what to do and by when
Under new and improved, in plain words
Recorded for the team, left out of the brief

scenarios.label: Bookings can be moved to another day
scenarios.why: A customer will notice it, and nothing breaks if they ignore it.

scenarios.label: Old booking links stop working
scenarios.why: A saved link will fail, so the customer needs to replace it before the date.

scenarios.label: Password reset email arrives faster
scenarios.why: A customer will notice it; nothing to do.

scenarios.label: Sign-in asks for an emailed code
scenarios.why: The customer needs access to the email address on the account, and must know before the day.

scenarios.label: Receipts no longer cut off long names
scenarios.why: A customer will notice it; nothing to do.
